description: 13.8 billion years ago, the universe started to expand. This is not a bomb going off in a void: space itself is what grows.

hero.hook: The Big Bang is not an explosion in space. It is space itself starting to grow.

blocks.text: **13.8 billion years** ago, everything that exists today was packed into an extremely dense, extremely hot state. Scientists sometimes call this beginning a [[singularity]]: a point where density and temperature are so extreme that our usual laws no longer describe the situation.

Then the universe began to expand. This is not a bomb throwing matter into a void that was already there. It is **space-time**, the fabric that ties space and time together, that grows and carries matter with it. That story is still going on today.

The name **“Big Bang”** is misleading. People often picture fireworks in the middle of an empty room. But before this event there is no room and no outside. Space and time as we know them begin with it. So asking “what came before?” gets very tricky: “before” no longer means the same thing.

blocks.caption: The expansion of the universe since the Big Bang

blocks.text: The term “Big Bang” was coined in **1949** by the British astrophysicist **Fred Hoyle**, who did not believe in it. He meant to mock the idea. The nickname stuck.

To picture the expansion, imagine dots drawn on a balloon. As the balloon inflates, every dot moves away from every other dot. No dot on the surface is “the center.” In the universe the idea is much the same: **galaxies**, huge collections of stars, drift apart because the space between them is stretching.

sections.title: Not an explosion in a void

blocks.text: In **1929**, the American astronomer **Edwin Hubble** found that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. So the universe is not fixed: it is growing. This is **Hubble's law**, the link between a galaxy's distance and its speed of retreat.

In **1965**, two engineers, **Arno Penzias** and **Robert Wilson**, picked up a radio hiss coming from every direction. It is the [[cosmic microwave background]]: a kind of thermal echo of the young universe, released when light could travel freely for the first time, about **380,000 years** after the start.
A small part of the “snow” on badly tuned old analog televisions came from this cosmic microwave background.

The third pillar is the proportion of the light elements. Calculations predict about **75%** hydrogen and **25%** helium formed in the first few minutes. Observations match those figures. This is [[primordial nucleosynthesis]], the forging of the first atomic nuclei in the minutes that follow the Big Bang.

Just after the start, the universe went through a phase of **inflation**, an extremely fast expansion lasting a fraction of a second. Then, around **3 minutes** in, **protons** and **neutrons**, the particles that make up atomic nuclei, came together as the first nuclei. For a long time the universe stayed like an opaque fog: light could not travel freely.

Around **380,000 years**, **electrons**, the light particles that orbit nuclei, joined the nuclei to form neutral atoms. Light broke free: that is the emission of the cosmic microwave background. The first stars were born much later, about **200 million years** after. Our own Sun appeared only **4.6 billion years** ago, out of matter recycled by earlier stars.
If the history of the universe fit into a single year, the Big Bang would happen on January 1 at midnight, and humanity would show up only at **11:52 p.m. on December 31**.

For a long time, people wondered whether gravity would eventually slow the expansion down. In **1998**, observations of distant [[supernovae]], exploding stars used as distance markers, showed the opposite: the [[accelerated expansion of the universe]]. A mysterious **dark energy**, a repulsive force that drives galaxies apart, seems to be pushing them, and it would account for about **68%** of the content of the universe. Ordinary matter, the kind that makes up our bodies, would be only about **5%**.

If this acceleration continues, the universe could drift toward extreme cold, an end sometimes nicknamed the **Big Freeze**. One thing is certain: what we see is only a portion of the whole. While light travels toward us, space keeps on stretching.

The Big Bang, **13.8 billion years** ago, was not an explosion in empty space: it is the expansion of space itself, confirmed by the flight of the galaxies, the cosmic microwave background, and the proportions of hydrogen and helium.
